passage: Since failing her accounts paper, Aparna had felt like wet cardboard. She went to her classes in the Delhi PG, came back, lay on the bed and scrolled until two. Her roommate Rehana didn't lecture her. One evening she just said, 'I'm walking to the chai stall. Ten minutes. Come if you want.' Aparna went, mostly so she wouldn't have to say no. The air was cool, and the stall owner's radio was playing old songs. It didn't fix anything. But on the way back, Aparna noticed she'd thought about the re-exam without dread for the first time in a week. They made it a habit: chai walk after dinner, most days. On the nights Aparna skipped it, Rehana just said, 'Tomorrow, then.' By the end of the month, Aparna had started planning her revision again.

'Bhaiya, it's seven. Weren't you going to the gym at five?'
'I didn't go, Shreya. I didn't go yesterday either.' Sumit pulled the blanket over his head. 'I'm useless.'

'Try it for a week.'
A week later, Sumit said, 'The walk's the only part of my day I don't dread.'

passage: Second year was the grey year for me. Nothing terrible happened. I just felt flat: slow in the mornings, foggy in lectures, stressed about everything and interested in nothing. Slowly I noticed the afternoon fog lifted a little after the walk. My notes got clearer. It didn't make the grey year sunny. It made it lighter. I still walk that loop when things feel heavy.

subtype: Overtraining and using exercise to escape [Actor]
passage: After I lost my job last year, I started running. At first it helped. Then it became two runs a day, morning and night, even in the rain, even with my knee strapped. If I missed one, I felt sick with guilt, like I'd let something terrible in. My friend Lavanya noticed first. 'Alka, you ran to my birthday dinner and left early to run again.' I laughed it off. Then I skipped my cousin's wedding because it clashed with a long run. That night, alone in my flat, I realised the running wasn't helping me live any more. It was running my life. I was running from worry, from the empty days. I told Lavanya the truth, and she helped me find a counsellor. I still run. Three times a week now, and I'm learning to sit with the worry instead.

Gym trainer's note, March
Jasleen has been coming in twice a day for three months, before and after work. I noticed she trains through pain, including last week with a swollen ankle. When the gym closed for Holi, she messaged me four times asking if there was any way in, and said she felt 'panicky' about missing a day. On Monday she mentioned that she hates how she looks and feels guilty if she eats out with friends. I didn't give her a new plan. I told her honestly that I was worried, that rest days are part of training, and that I thought she should talk to a doctor and a counsellor. She went quiet, then said, 'Maybe it's become a cage.' She has agreed to three sessions a week for now, and to see her doctor on Friday.
Deepak

Sunday night
Missed spin class today for Vinita's engagement. My own sister's engagement, and I spent half of it thinking about the class I'd skipped. I felt restless, like my skin was too tight, and I kept looking at my stomach in the mirror in the hall. Ate barely any of the food. Then I felt guilty for not enjoying the day, and guilty for not going to the gym. Guilty both ways. Driving home, I counted: I've trained every single day for five months. I've missed Nani's birthday lunch and two movie nights for it. That isn't health. That's fear. I'm writing it here so I can't pretend tomorrow. I'm going to tell the therapist on Tuesday exactly this. And I'm going to call Vinita and say sorry for being so distracted.
Indu

passage: Every January, Usha used to announce a plan: run five kilometres at six every morning. Every February, she'd quit and spend weeks feeling like a failure. This year, working at the bank in Bengaluru, she tried something different. She asked herself what she actually enjoyed. Badminton, she remembered, from school. Her colleague Joseph played at the club near the office, so she joined him on Tuesday and Friday evenings. On other days she got off the metro one stop early and walked. Sunday was rest, and she stopped treating it as cheating. 'Rest is part of it,' Joseph said. Some weeks she only managed one game. That was fine. By June, she was still playing, still laughing at her own missed shots, and for the first time the habit didn't come with guilt.

'Look, Lavanya. Thirty-day challenge. Two hours a day, no rest days.' Arnab held up his phone proudly.
'Two hours? You work till eight.'
'I'll sleep less. Go hard or go home.'
Lavanya laughed. 'I did that three times. Day nine, I'd be exhausted, skip once, feel terrible and quit.'
'So what do you do now? You go to that dance class, right?'
'Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday. I love it, so I actually go. And on Mondays I walk with my mum on the phone. That's it.'
'That's not much.'
'It's two years now. The thirty-day ones never lasted thirty days.'
Arnab frowned at the screen. 'And rest days?'
'Part of the plan. My body needs them.'
Arnab put the phone down. 'Maybe I'll start with football on Sundays.'

passage: Three New Years ago, I promised myself I'd go to the gym every single day. I lasted eleven days, then hid my membership card in a drawer and felt terrible every time I saw it. I'm Vidya, and it took me a while to figure out I don't like gyms. I like being outside. So now I cycle to the office on Mondays and Thursdays, when the traffic is kind. On Sundays I swim with my friend Baljeet at the municipal pool, mostly chatting between lengths. Wednesday and Saturday are rest days, and I've stopped calling them lazy days. Some weeks I only cycle once. I don't punish myself. It's been more than two years now, which is longer than any of my grand plans. I think the secret is simply that I look forward to it.

'Manoj, it's one o'clock.' Leela pulled back the curtains. Light poured across the unmade bed.
'Mumma! Close them!'
'You've had them shut for two weeks. You said yourself you feel like a zombie.'
'Because there's nothing to do in the holidays.'
'Or because you haven't seen daylight since Diwali.' Leela sat on the bed. 'You're grumpy, you're tired even after twelve hours, and yesterday you didn't know what day it was.'

'Deal. You get up at eight. We have chai on the balcony together, in the sun. Then do what you like.'

Four days later, Manoj was waiting on the balcony with two cups. 'Weird,' he said, squinting at the sun. 'I actually feel awake.'

Thursday
Six weeks into college in Pune, far from home, and today I felt steady for the first time. Wrote down why, so I don't forget.
The first month was chaos. Slept at random, skipped the mess, lay in bed missing everyone. So I've built a few anchors. Alarm at seven, every day, even Sunday. Walk to the tea stall by the gate before class. Breakfast, lunch and dinner at the mess at the proper times, even when I'm not that hungry. And Wednesday football with Pranav and the others from my floor, which I never skip. It sounds boring written down. But when the rest of life is brand new, these things stay the same, and that helps. Pranav said I look less lost.
Gurpreet

passage: When Nilesh moved from Nagpur to a small town near Wardha for his agriculture diploma, nothing was the same. The room above the grocery shop was noisy, the food was different, and he knew no one. For two weeks he slept late, skipped breakfast and spent evenings on his phone, feeling low. Then he made a plan. He set his alarm for six-thirty and walked to the river before class, watching the fishermen push off. He ate at the dhaba at the same times every day, so the owner started keeping his roti hot. And on Sundays he joined the bhajan group at the temple, where he met Ira, a classmate who sang loudly and badly. By the end of the month the town felt less strange, and so did he.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh walk before class?
qa.a: To the river.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel during the first two weeks?
qa.a: He felt low and lonely, knowing no one in a strange town.

qa.q: Which anchors helped Nilesh settle?
qa.a: A fixed wake-up time, a morning walk to the river, meals at the same times and Sunday bhajans.

qa.q: How might the dhaba owner have seen Nilesh?
qa.a: The owner probably saw a regular young customer and grew fond enough to keep his roti hot.

grounding: Shows a young adult away from home building anchors of wake time, a walk, regular meals and a weekly social activity that steady mood.

passage: Gargi, beti, you think this winter heaviness is only yours? Sit with your Akash Chacha a minute. When I was twenty-five, working in Delhi, every December the fog came and swallowed the sun for weeks. I'd wake in the dark, go to office in the dark, come home in the dark. By January I could barely drag myself out of bed. Food tasted of nothing. I stopped calling friends. Then March would come and I'd feel alive again. One winter it got so heavy I couldn't work. My friend Rakesh took me to a doctor, who listened carefully and helped me. After that I made rules: a walk at lunchtime in whatever light there was, bed and waking at fixed times, and a Sunday call with friends. Winters stayed grey. But never that heavy again.

qa.q: Where was Akash working at twenty-five?
qa.a: In Delhi.

qa.q: How did young Akash feel by January?
qa.a: He felt heavy and low, barely able to get out of bed, with food tasting of nothing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Akash's story?
qa.a: When the heaviness stopped him working, his friend Rakesh took him to a doctor, and he then built daily routines.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt seeing Akash that winter?
qa.a: Rakesh was probably worried and cared enough to take Akash to a doctor.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, low mood and energy in dark, foggy months that lift with brighter days, eased by getting outside, routines and a doctor.

passage: That winter in Shimla, the power went out almost every evening, and the sun barely cleared the hills before it sank again. Pooja, twenty-five, taught at a school on the ridge. By December she was exhausted all the time, craving sleep, and irritable with her students. She cried once in the staff room for no reason she could name. Her colleague Harsha noticed. 'You're not yourself. Is it the dark? I get it every year.' Harsha dragged her out for a walk in the noon sun every lunch break, even in the cold. Pooja kept her waking time fixed, even on Sundays. When the low mood still felt heavy after a month, she saw a doctor in town, who listened carefully and offered support. By February, as the days lengthened, Pooja felt her old energy returning.

qa.q: What went out almost every evening in Shimla?
qa.a: The power.

qa.q: How was Pooja feeling by December?
qa.a: She was exhausted, irritable and low, even crying without knowing why.

qa.q: What steps helped Pooja through the winter?
qa.a: Noon walks in the sun with Harsha, a fixed waking time and seeing a doctor when the low mood stayed heavy.

qa.q: How might Pooja's students have experienced her irritability?
qa.a: They may have felt confused or hurt by a usually kind teacher snapping at them.

grounding: Shows a young adult's energy and mood dipping in dark winter months, and getting outside, routines and a doctor's help as the sensible steps.

passage: The smog settled over Delhi in November, and with it came Joseph's familiar winter gloom. He woke tired, even after nine hours, and found himself dreading work he usually enjoyed. His wife, Parul, noticed he'd stopped playing his guitar in the evenings. 'You get like this every winter,' she said gently. 'And every spring you come back.' Joseph realised she was right. They made a plan together: breakfast on the balcony whenever there was light, a walk in Lodhi Garden at lunch, bed and wake times kept the same. Parul also suggested he see a doctor, since the low feeling had lasted weeks. The doctor listened and set up a follow-up. By mid-December, Joseph was still slower than in summer, but he picked up his guitar again.

qa.q: What had Joseph stopped doing in the evenings?
qa.a: Playing his guitar.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling as the smog settled in November?
qa.a: He felt tired and gloomy, dreading work he usually enjoyed.

qa.q: What sensible steps did Joseph take?
qa.a: Morning light on the balcony, lunchtime walks, fixed sleep times and seeing a doctor for the lasting low mood.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt seeing Joseph pick up his guitar again?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and happy to see a sign of his usual self.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing mood and energy dip in gloomy months, and getting outside, keeping routines and seeing a doctor as sensible steps.

passage: Mridul pushed the bhindi to the edge of his plate. 'Slimy,' he said, making a face. For months Zeenat had begged, then bribed with chocolate, then threatened no cartoons. Dinner had become a battle every night. This week she tried something else. She put one small piece of bhindi on his plate, said nothing about it and chatted about his day. Mridul ignored it. Next evening, another single piece, no fuss. On Friday he poked it. On Sunday he licked it and pulled a face. Zeenat just smiled. Two weeks later he ate a whole piece. 'It's still a bit slimy,' he announced, reaching for another.

qa.q: What did Mridul call the bhindi?
qa.a: Slimy.

qa.q: Why might Mridul have refused the bhindi so firmly?
qa.a: He disliked the slimy texture, and he probably felt pushed and stubborn when dinner became a battle.

qa.q: What did Zeenat change that worked?
qa.a: She stopped begging and bribing and calmly offered one small piece each day without fuss.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt during the months of battles?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and tired of every dinner turning into a fight.

grounding: Shows a young child refusing food because of texture and independence, and how calm, repeated offering without pressure widens his taste.

passage:
'Mehak, eat your dal. One more spoon and you get a chocolate.'
'NO! It's yucky!'
Sangeeta sighed. Every night was the same. Then she remembered what the doctor at the check-up had said. She put the spoon down. 'Okay. You don't have to eat it.'
Mehak looked suspicious. 'No chocolate?'
'No chocolate, no fighting. The dal is just there if you want it.'
Sangeeta ate her own dal and talked about the pigeon on the balcony.
Mehak watched. After a while, she dipped her roti in the dal. Just the edge.
'Hmm,' she said.
Sangeeta didn't cheer. She just kept talking about the pigeon.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta offer Mehak at first for eating dal?
qa.a: A chocolate.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when the bribes stopped?
qa.a: She was suspicious and curious, not sure what was happening.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta not cheer when Mehak dipped her roti?
qa.a: Making a fuss could have turned eating back into a contest; staying calm let Mehak try it on her own terms.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel as Mehak dips her roti?
qa.a: She is probably pleased and hopeful, but careful not to show it too much so the calm continues.

grounding: Shows a young child refusing food and a parent dropping bribes and pressure for calm offering, which lets the child try on her own.

passage:
Note from the preschool kitchen, Friday
For his first month here, Ojas ate only plain rice. Every day he pushed the vegetables away and cried if anyone coaxed him. We tried stickers; it made things worse. So we stopped. Now we put a small spoon of vegetables beside his rice each day and don't mention it. He sits with children who enjoy their food. On Monday he touched a carrot. Wednesday he sniffed it. Today he ate two pieces, then went back to rice. No one clapped. We'll keep offering, calmly. Please do the same at home; no pressure needed.
Sangeeta, kitchen staff

qa.q: What did Ojas eat for his first month?
qa.a: Only plain rice.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when people coaxed him to eat?
qa.a: He felt upset and pushed, crying when anyone coaxed him.

qa.q: Which approach worked better than stickers?
qa.a: Calmly offering a small spoon of vegetables daily without mentioning it.

qa.q: How might Ojas's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel hopeful and reassured that calm offering is working.

grounding: Shows a young child refusing many foods, and how dropping rewards and pressure for calm repeated offering slowly widens his taste.
